entries.definition: A conditional mixture-model family that organizes output experts as leaves of a tree and forms each leaf’s mixture weight by multiplying input-dependent probabilistic gates along its root-to-leaf path.

claims.statement: For input x and leaf l, define w_l(x) as the product of normalized child-gate probabilities along the path to l. Then p(y|x)=sum_l w_l(x) p_l(y|x). In the two-level presentation, p(y|x)=sum_i g_i(x) sum_j g_(j|i)(x) p_ij(y|x), with softmax gates and generalized-linear conditional expert densities. The conditional output mean is the corresponding weighted sum of expert means. Given an observed y, leaf responsibilities are proportional to w_l(x) p_l(y|x); they condition on both x and y, unlike input-only gates. Conditional EM alternates these responsibilities with weighted expert fits and gate fits to soft multinomial targets; a lower gate’s objective is weighted by the posterior probability of reaching its parent. The paper uses IRLS inside those maximum-likelihood subproblems. Its separate Algorithm 2 instead regresses log responsibilities by least squares, and its online variant uses discounted recursive weighted least squares. Those surrogate procedures are approximations to the specified fitting approach.

The optimized bound concerns log Z. It is an observed-data log-likelihood bound only when Z is that likelihood under the specified unnormalized posterior construction. A generic partition function is not automatically a probability of observations.

Coordinate ascent with exact factor optimization can improve the bound; arbitrary simultaneous field updates need not. The objective can have multiple stationary points, and neither global optimality nor accurate posterior marginals is guaranteed.
Omitted links inside one correlated substructure require the covariance/triple-moment terms of Equation (19); simply substituting independent means would change the derivation.

The auxiliary-variable equality in Equations (20)–(21) omits a coupling-dependent constant. For one binary edge K, a=acosh(exp(2*abs(K)))/2, b=sign(K)*a and C=exp(-abs(K))/2 give exp(K*s_i*s_j)=C*sum_w exp((a*s_i+b*s_j)*w). Dropping C preserves a normalized marginal but shifts the raw log partition; evidence bounds must retain the offset.

The context-sensitive HMM example has boundary conventions and a delayed observation term that need care; the displayed unary-field formula is not adopted as an implementation-ready recipe. Its synthetic illustration does not establish general weak-coupling accuracy or benchmark superiority.

claims.statement: For a fixed normalized target p(s)=exp(F(s))/Z and tractable q, maximize L(q)=E_q[F(s)]+H(q), so log Z-L(q)=KL(q||p). The source’s binary pairwise modular construction retains all intramodule interactions J and factorizes q across modules, replacing omitted intermodule interactions K by adjustable unary fields H. Expectations within a module are computed exactly using its tractable algorithm; expectations between modules factorize. A module’s field update is H_i^mu=h_i^mu+sum_(nu!=mu),j K_ij^(mu,nu) E_q[s_j^nu]. Holding all other factors fixed, recomputing that module with these fields gives a coordinate variational update. A chain module can use forward–backward while retaining within-chain correlations. If omitted links connect variables within the same correlated skeleton, the simple intermodule rule no longer follows: the source’s stationarity equations contain covariance and triple-moment terms. Auxiliary binary link variables provide another construction that induces a tractable core-versus-link factorization.

claims.statement: For a fixed target p(s)=exp(F(s))/Z, choose q(s)=product_i q_i(s_i) and maximize E_q[F]+H(q), equivalently minimizing KL(q||p). For the source’s binary s_i in {-1,+1} and F(s)=sum_(i<j) J_ij*s_i*s_j+sum_i h_i*s_i, write q_i(s_i)=(1+m_i*s_i)/2. Distinct-variable moments factor as E_q[s_i*s_j]=m_i*m_j, and entropy is the sum of the binary factor entropies. Interior stationarity gives atanh(m_i)=h_i+sum_(j!=i) J_ij*m_j, with symmetric interaction indexing. Updating one mean to tanh of that effective field while holding the others fixed solves its coordinate subproblem. These equations characterize the chosen approximate inference problem; they do not compute the exact target marginals in general.

limitations: Black box still requires sampling from and evaluating the variational distribution, score derivatives with respect to its parameters, and evaluation of the model log joint at sampled latent states. The method does not require differentiation through a discrete latent sample, but support and integrability conditions remain necessary.

Raw unbiasedness requires the regularity assumptions behind differentiation under the expectation and zero expected score. A model normalization constant independent of lambda cancels from this gradient; a parameter-dependent term cannot be discarded on that basis.

A coefficient fixed independently of the gradient samples preserves expectation when the relevant moments exist. A coefficient estimated from those same samples can correlate with the sample score and introduce bias. The paper reports separate sample counts for coefficient estimation and gradient calculation, but the inspected description does not establish an exact sampling-independence convention; no implementation behavior is asserted.

Population-optimal control-variate scaling and conditional-expectation variance reduction do not guarantee that estimated coefficients or every additional removal of zero-mean terms reduces finite-sample variance. Zero or poorly estimated score variance requires handling beyond division by the displayed ratio.

The practical step schedule and change-in-parameters stopping rule do not establish global optimality or exact posterior recovery. Mean-field factorization can limit the approximation. The printed hierarchical subsampling formulas need a separate weighting audit and are not curated as a verified extension here.

claims.statement: For fixed observed x and joint model p(x,z), choose a variational family q(z;lambda), sample z from q, and maximize L(lambda)=E_q[log p(x,z)-log q(z;lambda)] by stochastic ascent. Under the normalized-score and differentiation-under-expectation conditions, the raw gradient is E_q[grad_lambda log q(z;lambda)*(log p(x,z)-log q(z;lambda))], estimated by a Monte Carlo average. The mean-field version factors q into q_i(z_i;lambda_i) and uses for each factor the model log terms that depend on z_i together with -log q_i; unrelated terms cancel in expectation under the stated factorization. For parameter coordinate d in factor i, let h_d be the score and f_d be that score times the local log signal. A fixed control-variate coefficient gives f_d-a_d*h_d because E[h_d]=0; the population variance-minimizing coefficient is Cov(f_d,h_d)/Var(h_d) when these quantities exist and Var(h_d)>0. The source estimates coefficients from samples and averages corrected contributions before a stochastic-ascent update. Its fixed-coefficient expectation identity does not by itself justify arbitrary reuse of samples to estimate both the coefficient and corrected gradient.

claims.statement: For input x, a neural network outputs parameters defining p(t|x)=sum_i alpha_i(x) phi_i(t|x). In the report’s c-dimensional isotropic Gaussian construction, softmax outputs give nonnegative mixing weights summing to one, direct outputs give component means, and exponentiated outputs give positive standard deviations sigma_i, with covariance sigma_i squared times the identity. The mixture can have dependent target coordinates even though coordinates are independent within each isotropic component. Minimize the sum of negative log mixture densities over input/target pairs. With responsibilities r_i=alpha_i phi_i/p(t|x), the output-logit derivative of one negative log likelihood is alpha_i-r_i; the mean derivative is r_i(mu_i-t)/sigma_i squared and the log-scale derivative is r_i(c-||t-mu_i|| squared/sigma_i squared). Backpropagate these derivatives through the network. Mixture weights are conditional component priors before observing t; responsibilities condition on both x and t. The conditional mean is the weighted mean of component centers and need not be a mode or a plausible branch of a multivalued inverse mapping.
